say.text: Two patients, each with a first-part duodenal ulcer. Patient A has sudden epigastric pain, rigidity and free gas. Patient B has haematemesis and melaena, with no peritonitis.
Which is the posterior-wall ulcer, and what does it erode?

choices.label: Patient A, because the deeper wall perforates
Not sure, give me a hint
Patient B, eroding the gastroduodenal artery
Patient B, eroding the splenic artery

say.text: Ask what each ulcer's picture tells you it has opened into: the free belly, or a vessel.

choices.label: Try the question again

say.text: Yes. The posterior ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery and bleeds. The anterior ulcer breaks through into the free peritoneal cavity and causes peritonitis.

choices.label: Next

say.text: Naming the back wall as the deeper, more dangerous site feels right, because depth sounds like danger.
That is not right. Posterior ulcers bleed by eroding the gastroduodenal artery. It is the anterior ulcer that breaks through into the free peritoneal cavity.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which ulcer opens into the belly before you commit.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: A big upper-abdominal artery feels right, because the bleeder is near the stomach and the splenic artery is a familiar name.
That is not right. The posterior ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery, so the vessel is named by its duodenal position, not the spleen.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so name the artery that sits beside the first part of the duodenum.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: A duodenal ulcer perforates and spills its contents into the belly. The abdomen then changes over the next hours.
Which order do the stages follow?

choices.label: Bacterial peritonitis, then reaction, then chemical peritonitis
Chemical peritonitis, then reaction, then bacterial peritonitis
Not sure, give me a hint
Chemical peritonitis, then bacterial peritonitis, then reaction

say.text: Think about what the acid does in the first minutes, and what bacteria need hours to do.

choices.label: Try the question again

say.text: Yes. Acid, bile and enzymes cause chemical peritonitis first. Dilution then makes the patient look better, and bacteria take over as diffuse peritonitis.

choices.label: Next

say.text: Bacteria first feels right, because infection is what most people picture when a gut leaks.
That is not right. Acid, bile and enzymes spill first and cause chemical peritonitis. Bacteria arrive over hours.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace what leaks first, then what follows over hours.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Putting reaction last feels right, because the calm stage looks like the end of the illness.
That is not right. Reaction comes second. The exudate dilutes the irritant and the patient looks better, a lull before bacterial peritonitis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask whether the calm stage is recovery or a lull.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: A patient with colic writhes on the bed. A patient with a perforated ulcer lies almost still.
Why does the perforated patient keep still?

choices.label: Movement relieves peritoneal pain, so the rolling patient has peritonitis
Movement jars the inflamed peritoneum and worsens the pain
Not sure, give me a hint
Severe pain drives movement, so the still patient must have colic

say.text: Ask what movement does to an inflamed peritoneum, and what it does to a spasming gut.

choices.label: Try the question again

say.text: Yes. Inflamed peritoneum makes every movement jar, so the patient keeps still. The restless patient of colic is the reverse picture.

choices.label: Next

say.text: Movement easing pain feels right, because colic is the picture most people link with restlessness.
That is not right. Movement worsens peritoneal pain, so the perforated patient keeps still. The colic patient is the restless one.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what movement does to an inflamed peritoneum.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: More pain driving more movement feels right, because the most restless patient looks the sickest.
That is not right. Movement jars the inflamed peritoneum, so a still, rigid patient has peritonitis whatever the pain level.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what movement does to inflamed peritoneum, not how bad the pain looks.
